newsitem.title: EGYPT: Militant Islamists vow to attack Israel.
newsitem.headline: Militant Islamists vow to attack Israel.

text.p: Two militant Islamist groups vowed on Tuesday to carry out fresh suicide attacks inside Israel, deepening a crisis in the Middle East as a flurry of high-level meetings sought to revive a faltering peace process.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said after talks in Cairo with Israel's Foreign Minister David Levy he feared the latest crisis -- sparked by last week's suicide bombing in a Jerusalem market -- could lead to more violence if it was not resolved quickly.

He also told reporters it was "dangerous" to weaken Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's position. Israel cracked down on Palestinian self-rule areas after the bombing and said Arafat must do more to stamp out militant Moslem groups.

Arab League members held a meeting at their Cairo headquarters, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said Jordan's King Hussein would send his brother, Crown Prince Hassan, and Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali for talks with Netanyahu on Wednesday.

As diplomatic efforts to revive the peace process intensified ahead of a visit to the region by U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross, expected later this week, the military wing of the Islamic group Hamas promised a chain of attacks inside Israel.
"A chain of martyrdom attacks will come at the appropriate time to hit deep into Zionism," Hamas's Izz el-Deen al-Qassam Brigades said in a statement faxed to Reuters in Jerusalem.
"The Zionist entity state will become a state of frightened cowards that will know no rest or security," it said.

Another leaflet issued in Hamas's name last week claimed responsibility for the twin suicide attack that killed 15 people, including two bombers, and wounded 170 in Jerusalem's main Jewish market last Wednesday.
Hamas, which regards the Israel-PLO interim peace deals as a sell-out of their goal to found an Islamic state in Palestine, has in the past launched waves of suicide attacks in Israel.
In Nabatiyeh, southern Lebanon, the fundamentalist Moslem Shi'ite group Hizbollah buried five of its guerrillas killed by Israeli commandos and threatened to carry out suicide bombings inside Israel.

"Israel will witness explosions and suicide bombings inside all of its posts inside Palestine and inside occupied land," Hizbollah deputy secretary-general Naee'm Kassem told a crowd of several thousand at the fighters' funeral procession.

In a move that seemed sure to raise the political temperature still further, the Israeli group Peace Now said settlers had plans to double the number of housing units for Jews in the occupied West Bank.
The group said plans were at various stages of development to build an additional 44,089 units, equalling the number already built in all the Jewish settlements on the West Bank.
Mubarak, referring to Israel's move to seal off the West Bank and the Gaza Strip after the suicide bombings, said: "Weakening the position of Arafat is very, very dangerous in the peace process.
"We said that punishing the Palestinians -- no food, no medicine -- is very dangerous and may have very negative reactions, and I ask them to find a quick solution to the present situation..."

Arafat himself, speaking earlier in Amman after talks with King Hussein and other senior government officials, accused Netanyahu of wrecking the peace process and humiliating the Palestinians after the suicide bombings.

He told reporters Israel was exploiting the bombings to withdraw from its 1993 peace accords. The present Likud government in Israel inherited the accords reluctantly from the previous Labour administration.
The Palestinians broke off peace talks with Israel in March after the Israelis began construction of housing units for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem.

U.S. efforts to revive the peace process collapsed with the bombings in Jerusalem after which Netanyahu called a halt to peace talks and sealed off the Palestinian self-rule areas, disrupting Palestinian trade and barrings tens of thousands of Arabs from going to their workplaces in Israel.

Arafat said the peace accords "are not bilateral, they are international, and I want to say now there is an international responsibility falling on all those who signed these accord to move to save the peace process from the crisis which Netanyahu is pushing it daily towards."
